text: The evening stretched on considerably longer than anyone had properly planned for, Brother Crumb producing food in quantities that suggested he'd known, somehow, exactly how much celebrating this particular evening would require, Will peppering Pip with questions delivered in the tone of a man cataloguing an entirely new category of fact he intended to enjoy thoroughly.
“So when you beat me at cards that first winter,” Will said, “was that skill, or were you simply—”
“Skill,” Pip said, flatly. “I've beaten you at cards considerably more times than magic could possibly explain, Will. Some of us are simply better at cards than you.”
“That's rather a harder truth to accept than the wizard business, honestly.”
“He's taking this remarkably well,” Grimalkin observed, from his usual perch, watching the whole scene with dry satisfaction. “I rather expected more fainting.”
“Nobody in this camp faints properly anymore,” Barley said, mournfully. “I miss when things were more dramatic.”
“You could try fainting yourself, if you're so nostalgic for it.”
“I considered it. I decided the food was more interesting.”

Long John, meanwhile, had settled into an easy conversation with Thistlewood about nothing in particular — the weather, the coming season's harvest — with the simple, unhurried comfort of a man for whom nothing fundamental had actually shifted, whatever else the evening had revealed.

text: It was Marian who noticed first, catching Robin's eye across the crowded room with the particular quiet understanding that had become, over the past year, its own private language between them — and it was Robin who followed her lead a few minutes later, slipping away from the warmth and noise toward the cottage's quiet garden, where the evening air carried the season's last real warmth before autumn properly settled in.
“They didn't even notice us leaving,” Robin said, settling beside her on the low garden wall.
“They're rather thoroughly occupied,” Marian said. “Will's going to be insufferable about the cards thing for weeks, I expect.”

“Probably,” Robin agreed, and then, quieter, “I wanted a moment away from all of it. Not because the evening isn't wonderful. Simply because I find I wanted this part to belong to just the two of us.”
Marian looked at him for a long moment, something in her expression carrying all the careful weight of a year's worth of unstated things finally, deliberately, being allowed room to breathe.

“You said, this morning, that you wanted to be honest about rather more than the family's secret,” she said. “I've been thinking about that all day, rather more than I probably should have, given everything else we were meant to be managing.”
“And?” Robin asked, something hopeful and uncertain in his voice that he made no particular effort to hide.

“And I find I'm tired of filing things away for some safer day that never quite arrives,” Marian said, echoing her own words from that morning back at him, deliberate and plain. “I don't know what this is, exactly, or where it goes from here. I'm not certain either of us needs to know that tonight. But I wanted you to know, plainly, that I feel it too. Whatever it actually is.”

sequence._describe: Robin of Loxby and Marian Fletcher sharing a warm, gentle kiss in the quiet garden, soft evening light, a genuinely earned romantic moment. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. text: “That's rather a significant admission,” Robin said, quiet, something warm and unguarded working openly across his features now, no careful composure left to hide behind.
“It rather is,” Marian agreed. “I don't make them often. You may want to make note of the occasion.”

Robin laughed, soft and genuine, and in the small, easy silence that followed, something that had been building patiently across a year of careful glances and unstated warmth finally, gently, closed the distance between them — Marian leaning in first, or perhaps Robin did, neither of them particularly certain afterward which of them had properly started it, only that it felt, when it finally happened, like the most natural thing either of them had done in months.
When they finally drew back, neither rushed nor particularly eager to, Marian's expression carried something unguarded and genuinely happy that Robin had rarely seen from her before.
“Well,” she said, a little breathless, a little pleased with herself despite it. “That's rather more honesty than I generally manage in a single evening.”
“I'd say we've more than made up for a year's worth of careful restraint,” Robin said, warm.

“Let's not get ahead of ourselves,” Marian said, though there was no real caution in it, only the particular careful contentment of a woman who understood, plainly, that whatever came next didn't need deciding tonight. “One evening. One honest thing, properly finished, at last. The rest can wait for whenever it's actually ready to arrive.”

text: They returned to the cottage's warm, crowded gathering a while later, unhurried, neither particularly concerned about how obvious the change between them might be to anyone paying proper attention.
“There you two are,” Will said, catching sight of them with immediate, delighted suspicion. “You've got a look about you. The particular look.”
“We've no idea what you're referring to,” Marian said, entirely composed, though the small, private smile she and Robin exchanged rather thoroughly undercut the denial.
“Right,” Will said, grinning. “Well. I suppose that's simply one more thing this family's stopped keeping secrets about, then.”

The evening wound down slowly after that, warm and easy, the particular contented exhaustion of a family that had, at long last, set down every quiet corner it had been carrying — Thistlewood's magic, Pip's true self, and now, gently, unhurriedly, whatever Robin and Marian had finally allowed themselves to properly begin.

“Everyone knows everything now,” Robin said, later, watching the fire with Marian close beside him, the whole crew gathered easy and whole around them. “It's rather a strange feeling. Good. But strange.”

“Enjoy it while it lasts,” Marian said, quiet, some careful awareness working behind her contentment even now. “The world beyond this fire hasn't stopped turning simply because we've had a good evening. The Sheriff's still out there. Whatever's coming next hasn't waited politely for us to finish celebrating.”

“I know,” Robin said, and found, to his own quiet surprise, that the thought didn't frighten him nearly as much as it once might have. “But tonight, at least, we're facing whatever comes next as exactly who we actually are. All of us. Together. I find that's rather worth celebrating, whatever tomorrow eventually brings.”
